name: Regency

revival_periods.note: Regency Revival — the stuccoed, iron-balconied seaside and suburban manner of the interwar years, and the source of the American 'Regency Moderne' of the 1930s.

geography.hearth: Nash's London — Regent Street and the Regent's Park terraces — and the new resort towns of Brighton, Cheltenham, Leamington and Hove

lineage.note: Unbroken. The plan, the sash, the terrace, the leasehold building system and the trades are Georgian; Regency changes the surface, the roof line and the relation to the garden.
The thinning of every profile, the attenuated order and the taste for shaped rooms carry straight through from the Adam office into the Regency generation.
By the 1790s Adam's manner was being attacked as frippery and confectionery. The Greek turn is explicitly a demand for severity, mass and correctness against Adam's decorative delicacy.

Quoted from measured drawings, not descended from. Stuart and Revett's Antiquities of Athens, from 1762 onward, made the baseless Greek Doric column and the anthemion available to men who had never been to Greece, and Regency uses them as motifs on wholly English plans.

Directoire and Empire taste crosses the Channel through emigres, through Percier and Fontaine's plates, and through Thomas Hope's Household Furniture and Interior Decoration (1807). Regency interiors are as French as they are Greek.

description.short: Georgian construction rendered in stucco and opened to the garden: bow fronts, floor-length windows, cast-iron balconies under tented canopies, wide bracketed eaves, and Greek detail applied with a light hand.
description.long:
Regency is the moment the English house stops facing the street and starts facing the view. Almost everything structural is inherited — the brick carcass, the double-pile plan, the sash window, the terrace — but the priorities have shifted. Windows on the principal floor are taken down to the floor and turned into casements or long sashes opening onto a balcony, so that the drawing room and the garden become continuous; the front bows outward to catch a sea view or an oblique light; the roof, once hidden behind a parapet, comes out over the wall on brackets in a wide shallow overhang of Welsh slate. Underneath it all the brick is covered in stucco, ruled and lined to imitate ashlar and painted a pale stone colour. That last decision is the one everything else follows from: stucco is cheap, fast, moulds into any profile, and hides the fact that a magnificent terrace is a row of thin speculative shells.

The conditions are war, boom and leisure. The French wars cut off the Grand Tour and turned English travel inward, which built Brighton, Cheltenham, Leamington and Weymouth; peace and agricultural wealth after 1815 built the Regent's Park terraces; and the Prince Regent's own extravagance gave the period its name and its most conspicuous building. John Nash is the central figure not because he was the best architect of the period — Soane was, and knew it — but because he understood development. Regent Street, cut through London between 1811 and 1825, is simultaneously a piece of speculative real estate, a social boundary and a picturesque composition, and the Regent's Park terraces behind it dress rows of ordinary houses as single vast stuccoed palaces with giant orders and pediments. The trick is entirely scenographic and completely successful.

What Regency reacted against was Adam's prettiness, and what it reached for was severity — the baseless Greek Doric column, the plain incised anthemion, the unmoulded architrave. But it reached for a great deal else at the same time. The same decades produce the Royal Pavilion at Brighton, which is Indian outside and Chinese inside; the cottage orne with its thatch, tree-trunk verandas and diamond casements; Egyptian, Etruscan and Gothic rooms in the same house. Regency is where British classicism stops being a system and becomes a menu, and the eclecticism of the whole Victorian century starts here.

Standing in a Regency room is the first recognisably modern domestic experience in Britain. The window comes to the floor and the light is horizontal and abundant; you can walk out onto a balcony with a curved iron rail and a striped copper awning above it; the ceiling is plain or very lightly enriched; the walls are painted a strong flat colour; the furniture is light enough to be moved around the room rather than lined up against the walls. Outside, the stucco terrace works as a single wall of pale, softly modelled surface — bows, balconies and canopies casting shallow shadows — and it looks, correctly, like scenery. Nash was criticised in his own lifetime for building in lath and plaster; the buildings are still there, and still lovely, and still require repainting every few years.

defining_characteristics: Stuccoed walls, ruled and lined to imitate ashlar, painted in pale stone or cream, over a brick carcass
Bow, bay or canted fronts giving oblique views and modelling the terrace wall in shallow curves
Floor-length windows on the principal storey opening onto a cast-iron balcony, frequently under a tented copper canopy
Cast and wrought iron used as the principal ornament: balconies, verandas, railings, porches, in anthemion, lyre, heart and trellis patterns
Low-pitched hipped roofs of Welsh slate with wide overhanging eaves on plain or scrolled brackets, or alternatively a very shallow parapet
Greek rather than Roman detail, sparingly used: baseless Doric columns, incised anthemion and Greek key, unmoulded flat architraves
Very thin glazing bars, often with margin lights and occasionally coloured glass, and glazing patterns of 6-over-6, 3-over-6 or margin-light arrangements
diagnostic_tells: A cast-iron balcony with an ogee-tented copper hood over a floor-length window — the single most reliable Regency signature and one that appears in no earlier style
Stucco scored with ruled joints at the ground floor and left smooth above, so that a rendered wall imitates a rusticated base under ashlar
Wide eaves projecting 450-750 mm on brackets over a shallow slate roof, where Georgian would have a parapet or a modillion cornice tight to the wall
Glazing bars of 12-18 mm, thinner than anything before, sometimes with a narrow margin light framing the main panes
A Greek Doric porch with baseless, unfluted or partly fluted columns and a plain entablature, against the Roman Doric or Ionic doorcase of Georgian work

distinguished_from.difference: Material honesty is the dividing line. Georgian shows brick or ashlar and keeps its windows in the wall plane's discipline; Regency renders everything in stucco, bows the front, brings the windows to the floor, hangs ironwork on the facade and lets the eaves overhang. Georgian faces the street; Regency faces the garden.

Adam is Roman, floral, polychrome and interior-driven; Regency is Greek, linear, pale and exterior-driven. Adam thins the Georgian moulding; Regency deletes it — a Regency architrave is often a plain flat band with a single incised line.

The American cousin takes the Greek quotation far more literally, with full temple fronts, heavy pedimented gables and columns of structural scale, usually in painted wood. Regency uses Greek detail as light incident on a stuccoed box and rarely builds a full portico.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Georgian proportional habits, loosened and lightened, with Greek orders used as motifs rather than as a generative module. Composition is increasingly scenographic — the terrace or the villa is designed for how it reads from a moving viewpoint in a landscape.
typical_ratios: Ground-floor window 2:1 to 2.4:1 height to width, taken down to floor level; upper windows 1.6:1 to 1.8:1
Storey graduation retained: ground floor exceeds first by 10-15 percent, second floor 0.65-0.75 of the first
Eaves overhang 450-750 mm; roof pitch 22-30 degrees in slate
Bow front radius 3.5-6.0 m, projecting 0.6-1.2 m from the wall plane
Balcony depth 900-1200 mm, rail height 900-1050 mm
Greek Doric column height 6-7 diameters, baseless, with a plain unmoulded abacus
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even Georgian spacing, interrupted by the bow, which usually occupies the centre of a villa front or one end of a terrace unit. At the largest scale — Nash's Regent's Park terraces — a whole row is composed as a palace with a giant-order centre and end pavilions, and the individual house disappears entirely.

massing_affinities.note: The stuccoed terrace, palace-fronted or bow-fronted, is the style's defining urban form.
The Regency villa: a compact double-pile block with a hipped slate roof, wide eaves and a veranda, standing free in a small landscaped plot.
The standard terrace plan, unchanged from Georgian practice.
The full-width iron veranda, exported to and reimported from India and the colonies, makes the Regency villa a genuine gallery type in warm climates.
The castellated and Italianate villas of Nash and his contemporaries — Luscombe, Cronkhill — begin the picturesque asymmetrical house within an otherwise classical practice.

constraints.statement: Stucco must be continuous over all visible elevations of a rendered mass, with ruled ashlar lining confined to the ground storey where a rusticated base is intended. Stucco on the front with bare brick returns is forbidden.

Principal-floor windows extend to within 150 mm of the finished floor and open onto a balcony or veranda not less than 900 mm deep. A floor-length window with no balcony is a hazard and a period error.
Glazing bars 12-18 mm. Heavier bars date the work to before 1780; the thin bar is what makes a Regency window read as a sheet of light.

Where wide eaves are used they project 450-750 mm on visible brackets or a plain soffit, and the roof pitch stays between 22 and 30 degrees in slate. A steep roof under wide eaves belongs to the Italianate, forty years later.
Greek and Roman detail may not be mixed on one elevation. Exotic modes — Indian, Egyptian, Chinese, Gothic — are permitted but must be complete within a room or a whole building, never blended.

exemplars.name: Cumberland Terrace
exemplars.note: Designed by John Nash and executed by James Thomson. A row of ordinary houses fronted as a single stuccoed palace with a giant Ionic order and a sculptured pediment — the scenographic method at full strength.

exemplars.name: Royal Pavilion
exemplars.note: Remodelled by Nash 1815-23 for the Prince Regent from Henry Holland's earlier villa. Indian outside, Chinese inside, and structurally a cast-iron frame — the period's eclecticism and its technology in one building.

exemplars.name: Park Crescent
exemplars.note: Built 1806-21 by Nash. A semicircular stuccoed crescent with a continuous paired Ionic colonnade at ground level, and the hinge between Portland Place and Regent's Park.

exemplars.name: Sir John Soane's Museum, 12-14 Lincoln's Inn Fields
exemplars.note: Built and rebuilt by Soane for himself 1792-1824. The period's other pole: incised linear ornament, top-lit spaces, mirrors and shallow domes, and a classicism reduced almost to abstraction.
